input.question: If Germany wasn't a country at the time, how come Martin Luther was considered German? What nationality would he have been considered at the time?
input.ground_truth: Germanic was an ethnic group long before the company of Germany was formed. Germany is really just the latest iteration in a chain of German countries in that area of the world. The Holy Roman Empire was the first "germany", but even before that the Romans would refer to that part of the world as Germania.

Question: If Germany wasn't a country at the time, how come Martin Luther was considered German? What nationality would he have been considered at the time?

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a big family, but your family’s house (the country) doesn’t have a name yet, or it’s not officially a house—it’s just a bunch of people living together.

Martin Luther was born in a place we now call Germany, but back then, that place didn’t have a name like “Germany.” Instead, it was a bunch of little kingdoms and cities, kind of like different rooms in a big house.

So, Martin Luther was from a place called Saxony, which was like one room in that big house. People would say he was from Saxony, or maybe “Saxon,” or sometimes just “a German” if they meant someone from that area.

But he wasn’t called “German” in the way we use it today, because “Germany” as a country didn’t exist yet. He was a Saxon, or maybe just someone from “the lands of the Holy Roman Empire,” which was like the name of the whole big house.

So, if someone asked, “What are you?” Martin Luther would probably say, “I’m from Saxony!” or “I’m a Saxon.” That’s like saying, “I’m from Texas!” instead of just “I’m American,” if Texas was its own little place.
